claim: Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is the predominant pathway that repairs DNA double-strand breaks in vertebrates.
source: Non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) is the predominant pathway that repairs DNA double-strand breaks in vertebrates.
evidence: Supported by citation to Rothkamm et al., 2003

claim: During NHEJ DNA ends are held together by a multi-protein synaptic complex until they are ligated.
source: During NHEJ DNA ends are held together by a multi-protein synaptic complex until they are ligated.
evidence: Established understanding of NHEJ mechanism

claim: The XLF tail along with the Ku-binding motif (KBM) at the extreme C-terminus are required for end joining.
source: We demonstrate that the XLF tail along with the Ku-binding motif (KBM) at the extreme C-terminus are required for end joining.
evidence: Demonstrated through ensemble end joining assays in Xenopus egg extract and cellular assays

claim: Although the underlying sequence of the tail can be varied, a minimal tail length is required for NHEJ.
source: Although the underlying sequence of the tail can be varied, a minimal tail length is required for NHEJ.
evidence: Demonstrated through shuffled tail mutants and truncation mutants in end joining assays

claim: The defect in XLF tail truncation mutants is due to a failure to closely align DNA ends.
source: Single-molecule FRET experiments that observe end synapsis in real-time show that this defect is due to a failure to closely align DNA ends.
evidence: Demonstrated through single-molecule FRET experiments showing reduced SR complex formation rates

claim: A single C-terminal tail tethers XLF to Ku, while allowing XLF to form interactions with XRCC4 that enable synaptic complex formation.
source: Our data supports a model in which a single C-terminal tail tethers XLF to Ku, while allowing XLF to form interactions with XRCC4 that enable synaptic complex formation.
evidence: Supported by data from asymmetric XLF mutants and heterodimers showing single KBM is sufficient

claim: Within vertebrates the majority of DSBs are repaired by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ).
source: Within vertebrates the majority of DSBs are repaired by non-homologous end joining (NHEJ) (Rothkamm et al., 2003).
evidence: Supported by citation to Rothkamm et al., 2003

claim: NHEJ does not use a DNA template to guide repair.
source: In contrast to homologous recombination (HR), the other major DSB repair pathway, NHEJ does not use a DNA template to guide repair.
evidence: Established characteristic distinguishing NHEJ from HR

claim: Ku rapidly binds DNA ends.
source: Recognition of the DSB is carried out by the ring-shaped Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer (Ku) which rapidly binds DNA ends (Walker et al., 2001)
evidence: Supported by citation to Walker et al., 2001

claim: Ku recruits DNA-PKcs.
source: Recognition of the DSB is carried out by the ring-shaped Ku70/Ku80 heterodimer (Ku) which rapidly binds DNA ends (Walker et al., 2001) and subsequently recruits downstream NHEJ factors including the DNA-dependent protein kinase catalytic subunit, DNA-PKcs (Uematsu et al., 2007; Jette and Lees-Miller, 2015)
evidence: Supported by citations to Uematsu et al., 2007 and Jette and Lees-Miller, 2015

claim: DNA-PKcs kinase activity is essential for DNA repair.
source: the DNA-dependent protein kinase catalytic subunit, DNA-PKcs (Uematsu et al., 2007; Jette and Lees-Miller, 2015), whose kinase activity is essential for DNA repair (Jiang et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Jiang et al., 2015

claim: DNA ends are often initially incompatible with ligation.
source: As DSBs arise from a wide-range of sources, DNA ends are often initially incompatible with ligation.
evidence: General knowledge about DSB heterogeneity

claim: NHEJ-associated polymerases and nucleases act on DNA ends to allow for ligation by DNA ligase IV.
source: A host of end processing enzymes, including NHEJ-associated polymerases and nucleases, act on these ends to allow for ligation by DNA ligase IV (Lig4) (Grawunder et al., 1997; Stinson et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grawunder et al., 1997 and Stinson et al., 2020

claim: Ligation requires XRCC4, Lig4, and XLF.
source: Ligation requires at least two additional factors: XRCC4, a scaffolding factor to which Lig4 is constitutively bound and the structurally related XRCC4-like factor (XLF) (Grawunder et al., 1997; Buck et al., 2006; Ahnesorg et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by citations to Grawunder et al., 1997; Buck et al., 2006; Ahnesorg et al., 2006

claim: There are at least two distinct synaptic states that precede ligation during NHEJ.
source: Using single-molecule Förster resonance energy transfer (smFRET) experiments to monitor the distance between DNA ends in Xenopus laevis egg extract, we have shown that there are at least two distinct synaptic states that precede ligation (Graham et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Graham et al., 2016 and prior smFRET experiments

claim: Ku and DNA-PKcs (but not kinase activity) are required to form the long-range (LR) complex.
source: First, Ku and DNA-PKcs (but not kinase activity) are required to weakly tether DNA ends at a distance where they are protected from processing, a state we named the long-range (LR) complex (Stinson et al., 2020; Graham et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stinson et al., 2020 and Graham et al., 2016

claim: DNA-PKcs kinase activity, XRCC4, Lig4, and XLF are required to transition from the LR complex to the SR complex.
source: Next, DNA-PKcs kinase activity, XRCC4, Lig4, and XLF are required to transition from the initial LR complex to a stable short-range (SR) synaptic complex in which the DNA ends are closely aligned for processing and ligation (Stinson et al., 2020; Graham et al., 2016).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stinson et al., 2020 and Graham et al., 2016

claim: The catalytic activity of Lig4 is not required to form the SR complex.
source: Importantly, the catalytic activity of Lig4 is not required to form the SR complex, demonstrating that the ligase plays a structural role in end synapsis (Graham et al., 2016; Cottarel et al., 2013).
evidence: Supported by citations to Graham et al., 2016 and Cottarel et al., 2013

claim: The architecture of the NHEJ synaptic complex is conserved from Xenopus to humans.
source: Subsequent biochemical reconstitutions of human NHEJ proteins also found evidence for these two synaptic states (Wang et al., 2018), suggesting that the architecture of the NHEJ synaptic complex is conserved from Xenopus to humans.
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang et al., 2018 and inference from comparative data

claim: XLF, XRCC4, and PAXX exist as homodimers.
source: XLF, as well as the structurally similar XRCC4 and PAXX, exist as homodimers (Xing et al., 2015; Ochi et al., 2015; Li et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Xing et al., 2015; Ochi et al., 2015; Li et al., 2008

claim: XLF, XRCC4, and PAXX consist of an N-terminal globular head domain, an extended coiled-coil stalk that mediates dimerization, and a flexible C-terminal tail.
source: Each of these paralogues consists of an N-terminal globular head domain, an extended coiled-coil stalk that mediates dimerization (Li et al., 2008), and a flexible C-terminal tail (Figure 1A; Andres et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Li et al., 2008 and Andres et al., 2007, and shown in Figure 1A

claim: XLF and XRCC4 interact through their head domains.
source: XLF and XRCC4 interact through their head domains (Andres et al., 2012; Malivert et al., 2010)
evidence: Supported by citations to Andres et al., 2012 and Malivert et al., 2010

claim: The XLF-XRCC4 interaction is essential for NHEJ in cells.
source: and this interaction is essential for NHEJ in cells (Roy et al., 2015; Roy et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Roy et al., 2015 and Roy et al., 2012

claim: XLF and XRCC4 can form extensive filaments in minimal reconstitutions.
source: In minimal reconstitutions of XRCC4 and XLF, this interaction can lead to the formation of extensive XLF-XRCC4 filaments (Andres et al., 2012; Ropars et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citations to Andres et al., 2012 and Ropars et al., 2011

claim: XLF-XRCC4 filaments have been proposed to be important for repair in vivo.
source: which have been proposed to be important for repair in vivo (Mahaney et al., 2013; Reid et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Mahaney et al., 2013 and Reid et al., 2015

claim: A single XLF dimer is sufficient for SR complex formation.
source: However, single-molecule imaging of fluorescently labeled XLF in egg extract by our laboratory revealed that a single XLF dimer is sufficient for SR complex formation, although it must interact with XRRC4 through both of its head domains for optimal end joining (Graham et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Graham et al., 2018 and prior single-molecule imaging experiments

claim: XLF must interact with XRCC4 through both of its head domains for optimal end joining.
source: However, single-molecule imaging of fluorescently labeled XLF in egg extract by our laboratory revealed that a single XLF dimer is sufficient for SR complex formation, although it must interact with XRRC4 through both of its head domains for optimal end joining (Graham et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Graham et al., 2018

claim: A single XLF dimer makes several contacts within the SR complex to mediate synapsis.
source: These results suggest that a single XLF dimer makes several contacts within the SR complex to mediate synapsis.
evidence: Inference from single-molecule imaging data

claim: XLF contains an extended intrinsically disordered C-terminal tail with a highly conserved Ku-binding motif (KBM) at the terminus.
source: XLF contains an extended intrinsically disordered C-terminal tail with a highly conserved Ku-binding motif (KBM) at the terminus (Figure 1A–B; Yano et al., 2011; Nemoz et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Yano et al., 2011 and Nemoz et al., 2018, and shown in Figure 1A-B

claim: Deletion of the KBM ablates cellular recruitment of XLF to sites of DNA damage.
source: Deletion of the KBM ablates cellular recruitment of XLF to sites of DNA damage (Yano et al., 2011)
evidence: Supported by citation to Yano et al., 2011

claim: Mutations within the KBM result in varying defects in cellular end joining assays and cell survival in the presence of DSB inducing agents.
source: and mutations within the KBM result in varying defects in cellular end joining assays and cell survival in the presence of DSB inducing agents (Nemoz et al., 2018; Bhargava et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Nemoz et al., 2018 and Bhargava et al., 2018

claim: There is poor sequence conservation within the XLF tail region across vertebrate species.
source: Across vertebrate species, there is poor sequence conservation within this region, and yet the tail is invariably retained with a similar length (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A through sequence alignment

claim: The XLF tail is invariably retained with a similar length across vertebrate species.
source: Across vertebrate species, there is poor sequence conservation within this region, and yet the tail is invariably retained with a similar length (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A through sequence alignment

claim: The XLF tail is a target for phosphorylation by DNA-PKcs.
source: although it has been shown to be a target for phosphorylation by DNA-PKcs (Yu et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yu et al., 2008

claim: Deleting the entire C-terminal region of XLF (including the KBM) still allows for interaction with XRCC4.
source: Deleting the entire C-terminal region of XLF (including the KBM) still allows for interaction with XRCC4 (Andres et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citation to Andres et al., 2007

claim: The C-terminal region of XLF is necessary for an interaction with DNA in vitro.
source: However, minimal reconstitutions show that the C-terminal region of XLF is necessary for an interaction with DNA in vitro (Andres et al., 2007; Andres et al., 2012)
evidence: Supported by citations to Andres et al., 2007 and Andres et al., 2012

claim: The C-terminal region of XLF variably stimulates (1.5–40 fold) end joining in minimal reconstitutions.
source: and variably stimulates (1.5–40 fold) end joining (Wang et al., 2018; Andres et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang et al., 2018 and Andres et al., 2007

claim: Immunodepletion of XLF from extract abolished end joining.
source: Immunodepletion of XLF from extract (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B) abolished end joining (Figure 1C), consistent with prior results in extract and in cells (Graham et al., 2016; Roy et al., 2015).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1C and supported by citations to Graham et al., 2016 and Roy et al., 2015

claim: A mock immunodepletion did not alter end joining.
source: A mock immunodepletion did not alter end joining, and joining in XLF-depleted extract was rescued by adding back physiological concentrations (~75 nM; Wühr et al., 2014) of recombinant wild type (wt) XLF (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1C and physiological concentration supported by citation to Wühr et al., 2014

claim: Joining in XLF-depleted extract was rescued by adding back physiological concentrations (~75 nM) of recombinant wild type XLF.
source: A mock immunodepletion did not alter end joining, and joining in XLF-depleted extract was rescued by adding back physiological concentrations (~75 nM; Wühr et al., 2014) of recombinant wild type (wt) XLF (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1C and physiological concentration supported by citation to Wühr et al., 2014

claim: XLFΔKBM did not rescue end joining in XLF-depleted extract.
source: Notably, an XLF mutant lacking the KBM, XLFΔKBM, did not rescue end joining in XLF-depleted extract, demonstrating that the KBM is necessary for end joining (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1C

claim: The KBM is necessary for end joining.
source: Notably, an XLF mutant lacking the KBM, XLFΔKBM, did not rescue end joining in XLF-depleted extract, demonstrating that the KBM is necessary for end joining (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1C

claim: Wild type XLF was able to robustly rescue joining at sub-nanomolar concentrations.
source: While wt XLF was able to robustly rescue joining at sub-nanomolar concentrations, the XLFΔKBM supported little end joining even at micromolar concentrations.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1D titration experiment

claim: XLFΔKBM supported little end joining even at micromolar concentrations.
source: While wt XLF was able to robustly rescue joining at sub-nanomolar concentrations, the XLFΔKBM supported little end joining even at micromolar concentrations.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1D titration experiment

claim: The KBM plays a critical role in recruiting XLF to DSBs through its interaction with Ku.
source: Collectively, these results are consistent with the KBM playing a critical role in recruiting XLF to DSBs through its interaction with Ku (Yano et al., 2011; Nemoz et al., 2018).
evidence: Inference from experimental data and supported by citations to Yano et al., 2011 and Nemoz et al., 2018

claim: XLF1-265+KBM and XLF1-245+KBM showed no significant joining activity at 75 nM.
source: At 75 nM the more severe truncations, XLF1-265+KBM and XLF1-245+KBM, showed no significant joining activity, while the most conservative truncation, XLF1-285+KBM, was able to rescue end joining.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2B

claim: XLF1-285+KBM was able to rescue end joining at 75 nM.
source: At 75 nM the more severe truncations, XLF1-265+KBM and XLF1-245+KBM, showed no significant joining activity, while the most conservative truncation, XLF1-285+KBM, was able to rescue end joining.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2B

claim: Joining by XLF1-245+KBM was barely detectable at 500 nM.
source: Even at a concentration of 500 nM, joining by XLF1-245+KBM was barely detectable while joining by XLF1-265+KBM was clearly much slower than the wild type.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Joining by XLF1-265+KBM was clearly much slower than the wild type at 500 nM.
source: Even at a concentration of 500 nM, joining by XLF1-245+KBM was barely detectable while joining by XLF1-265+KBM was clearly much slower than the wild type.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: Joining by XLF1-285+KBM was similar to the wild type at 500 nM.
source: In contrast, joining by XLF1-285+KBM was similar to the wild type (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A

claim: The melting temperatures (Tm) of the XLF truncation mutants were similar to the Tm of wt XLF.
source: Consistent with all three mutants being stably folded, we found that the melting temperatures (Tm) of the mutants were similar to the Tm of wt XLF.
evidence: Demonstrated by differential scanning fluorimetry in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B

claim: The tail of XLF is required for efficient end joining in egg extract.
source: Thus, the tail of XLF is required for efficient end joining in egg extract.
evidence: Conclusion from truncation mutant experiments

claim: The SR complex formation rate for wt XLF is 1.7 × 10−3 ± 3.4 × 10−4 s−1.
source: The SR complex formation rate for wt XLF (1.7 × 10−3 ± 3.4 × 10−4 s−1) agrees well with a previously published value (Graham et al., 2018)
evidence: Measured from single-molecule FRET experiments and agrees with citation to Graham et al., 2018

claim: The SR complex formation rates for the buffer and XLF1-245+KBM conditions were > 25 fold lower than wt XLF.
source: while the rates for the buffer and XLF1-245+KBM conditions were > 25 fold lower, at 6.4 × 10−5 ± 1.0 × 10−5 s−1 and 4.6 × 10−5 ± 1.3 × 10−5 s−1, respectively (Figure 3G).
evidence: Measured from single-molecule FRET experiments shown in Figure 3G

claim: XLF1-245+KBM is deficient in forming the SR complex.
source: As we observed a similarly low number of high FRET events (SR complex formation) for the buffer and XLF1-245+KBM conditions (Supplementary file 1), these results show that XLF1-245+KBM is deficient in forming the SR complex.
evidence: Demonstrated by single-molecule FRET experiments

claim: The tail of XLF is required for formation of the SR complex and the close alignment of DNA ends.
source: Collectively, these results indicate that the tail of XLF is required for formation of the SR complex and the close alignment of DNA ends.
evidence: Conclusion from single-molecule FRET experiments

claim: XLFNoPhos+KBM was able to rescue end joining in XLF-depleted extract as efficiently as wt XLF.
source: This mutant, XLFNoPhos+KBM, was able to rescue end joining in XLF-depleted extract as efficiently as wt XLF (Figure 4A), consistent with XLF phosphorylation not being required for end synapsis and ligation.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 4A

claim: XLF phosphorylation is not required for end synapsis and ligation.
source: This mutant, XLFNoPhos+KBM, was able to rescue end joining in XLF-depleted extract as efficiently as wt XLF (Figure 4A), consistent with XLF phosphorylation not being required for end synapsis and ligation.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 4A and inference from XLFNoPhos+KBM rescue

claim: XLFShuffA+KBM and XLFShuffB+KBM rescued end joining in XLF-depleted extract with wild type-like efficiency.
source: We constructed two distinct shuffled mutants using this approach, XLFShuffA+KBM and XLFShuffB+KBM (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A), and each of these mutants rescued end joining in XLF-depleted extract with wild type-like efficiency (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 4A

claim: The loss of phosphorylation sites or disruption of a required motif within the tail is not the cause of the end joining defect exhibited by the truncation mutants.
source: Collectively, these results rule out the loss of phosphorylation sites or disruption of a required motif within the tail as the cause of the end joining defect exhibited by the truncations mutants.
evidence: Conclusion from XLFNoPhos+KBM and shuffled mutant experiments

claim: Robust end joining was observed when tdXLFWT/WT or tdXLFΔKBM/WT were used to rescue XLF-depleted egg extract.
source: Robust end joining was observed when tdXLFWT/WT or tdXLFΔKBM/WT were used to rescue XLF-depleted egg extract, but little to no joining was observed with either tdXLFWT/ΔKBM or tdXLF ΔKBM /ΔKBM (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 4C

claim: Little to no joining was observed with either tdXLFWT/ΔKBM or tdXLFΔKBM/ΔKBM.
source: Robust end joining was observed when tdXLFWT/WT or tdXLFΔKBM/WT were used to rescue XLF-depleted egg extract, but little to no joining was observed with either tdXLFWT/ΔKBM or tdXLF ΔKBM /ΔKBM (Figure 4C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 4C

claim: A single KBM within an XLF dimer is sufficient for XLF's role in promoting end joining in extracts.
source: Since we see robust joining with tdXLFΔKBM/WT and tdXLFL301E/WT, these results demonstrate that a single KBM within an XLF dimer is sufficient for XLF's role in promoting end joining in extracts.
evidence: Demonstrated by tandem dimer experiments in Figure 4C and Figure 4—figure supplement 2A

claim: Flag-Avi-XLF/His10-XLFΔtailΔKBM and Flag-Avi-XLF/His10-XLF can rescue end joining in XLF-depleted extracts.
source: A comparison of joining efficiency for the Flag-Avi-XLF/His10-XLFΔtailΔKBM construct and the wild-type Flag-Avi-XLF/His10-XLF revealed that both constructs can rescue end joining in XLF-depleted extracts, whereas dimers of His10-XLFΔtailΔKBM cannot (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 4E

claim: Dimers of His10-XLFΔtailΔKBM cannot rescue end joining in XLF-depleted extracts.
source: A comparison of joining efficiency for the Flag-Avi-XLF/His10-XLFΔtailΔKBM construct and the wild-type Flag-Avi-XLF/His10-XLF revealed that both constructs can rescue end joining in XLF-depleted extracts, whereas dimers of His10-XLFΔtailΔKBM cannot (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 4E

claim: The linear substrate persisted at later times in the Flag-Avi-XLF/His10-XLFΔtailΔKBM rescue relative to Flag-Avi-XLF/His10-XLF.
source: However, the linear substrate persisted at later times in the Flag-Avi-XLF/His10-XLFΔtailΔKBM rescue relative to Flag-Avi-XLF/His10-XLF (Figure 4E).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 4E

claim: Flag-Avi-XLF/His10-XLFΔtailΔKBM forms the SR complex less efficiently than Flag-Avi-XLF/His10-XLF.
source: Consistent with these observations, a comparison of these same constructs using the smFRET SR complex formation assay showed that while both Flag-Avi-XLF/His10-XLFΔtailΔKBM and Flag-Avi-XLF/His10-XLF form the SR complex, Flag-Avi-XLF/His10-XLFΔtailΔKBM does so less efficiently (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–D).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 4—figure supplement 3A–D

claim: A single KBM on a single tail of XLF is sufficient for robust end joining.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate that a single KBM on a single tail of XLF is sufficient for robust end joining.
evidence: Conclusion from heterodimer experiments

claim: The XLF-XRCC4 interaction is required for SR complex formation.
source: Previously, we showed that the XLF-XRCC4 interaction is required for SR complex formation (Graham et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Graham et al., 2018

claim: Robust recruitment of the core NHEJ factors Ku, DNA-PKcs, XRCC4, Lig4, and XLF was observed in the mock-depleted extract relative to the uncut control DNA.
source: Robust recruitment of the core NHEJ factors Ku, DNA-PKcs, XRCC4, Lig4, and XLF was observed in the mock-depleted extract relative to the uncut control DNA (Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5B DNA pulldown experiment

claim: The lower electrophoretic mobility of XRCC4 and XLF is likely due to phosphorylation by DNA-PKcs.
source: Consistent with previous reports, the lower electrophoretic mobility of XRCC4 and XLF is likely due to phosphorylation by DNA-PKcs (Cottarel et al., 2013; Yu et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cottarel et al., 2013 and Yu et al., 2008

claim: Loss of XLF led to a large reduction in XRCC4 and Lig4 signal that could be rescued by addition of recombinant wild type XLF.
source: To determine if XLF is required to stabilize XRCC4-Lig4 at DNA ends, we depleted XLF from egg extract and then blotted for NHEJ factors in our pulldown assay. Loss of XLF led to a large reduction in XRCC4 and Lig4 signal that could be rescued by addition of recombinant wild type XLF.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5B DNA pulldown experiment

claim: The interaction between XLF and XRCC4 stabilizes the XRCC4-Lig4 complex at DNA ends.
source: As XRCC4-Lig4 is known to be recruited in the absence of XLF (Wu et al., 2007), these results are consistent with the interaction between XLF and XRCC4 stabilizing the XRCC4-Lig4 complex at DNA ends.
evidence: Inference from DNA pulldown data and supported by citation to Wu et al., 2007

claim: XLFL117D was associated with DNA ends yet could not restore XRCC4-Lig4 stability.
source: We next tested XLFL117D (human XLFL115D), an XRCC4 interaction deficient mutant (Graham et al., 2018). XLFL117D was associated with DNA ends yet could not restore XRCC4-Lig4 stability (Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5B DNA pulldown experiment

claim: XLF1-245+KBM failed to restore XRCC4-Lig4 stability even though it was robustly recruited.
source: Similarly, XLF1-245+KBM failed to restore XRCC4-Lig4 stability even though it was robustly recruited.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 5B DNA pulldown experiment

claim: A minimal tail length is necessary for XLF to stabilize the XRCC4-Lig4 complex.
source: Collectively, these results show that a minimal tail length is necessary for XLF to stabilize the XRCC4-Lig4 complex.
evidence: Conclusion from DNA pulldown experiments

claim: Error-free end joining in the EJ7-GFP assay depends solely on canonical NHEJ factors.
source: With this assay, error-free end joining depends solely on canonical NHEJ factors (Figure 6A; Bhargava et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Bhargava et al., 2018

claim: GFP+ cells are dependent on XLF in the EJ7-GFP assay.
source: As previously observed, GFP+ cells are dependent on XLF in that transfections with wt XLF causes a high frequency of GFP+ cells (~50%), but without XLF (i.e. empty vector) GFP+ cells are near background levels (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6B cellular assay

claim: The XLF KBM and tail are both important for efficient end joining in cells.
source: Similar to our results in Xenopus egg extract we observed that the XLF KBM and tail were both important for efficient end joining in cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6B cellular assay

claim: XLFΔKBM led to a severe joining defect (sixfold) compared to wt XLF in cells.
source: As compared to wt XLF, XLFΔKBM led to a severe joining defect (sixfold), and XLF1-243+KBM led to a substantial reduction (3.2-fold).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6B cellular assay

claim: XLF1-243+KBM led to a substantial reduction (3.2-fold) in end joining compared to wt XLF in cells.
source: As compared to wt XLF, XLFΔKBM led to a severe joining defect (sixfold), and XLF1-243+KBM led to a substantial reduction (3.2-fold).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6B cellular assay

claim: Transfection of tdXLF(WT/WT) and tdXLF(ΔKBM/WT) rescued repair as efficiently as wt XLF in cells.
source: Consistent with our results in egg extract, transfection of tdXLF(WT/WT) and tdXLF(ΔKBM/WT) rescued repair as efficiently as wt XLF.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6B cellular assay

claim: tdXLF(ΔKBM/ΔKBM) showed a severe defect compared to wt XLF (12.2-fold) in cells.
source: However, tdXLF(ΔKBM/ΔKBM) showed a severe defect compared to wt XLF (12.2-fold).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6B cellular assay

claim: A single KBM within an XLF dimer is sufficient for end joining in cells.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate that a single KBM within an XLF dimer is sufficient for end joining in cells, but the tail of XLF must be sufficiently long to facilitate efficient end joining.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6B cellular assay

claim: The tail of XLF must be sufficiently long to facilitate efficient end joining in cells.
source: Overall, these results demonstrate that a single KBM within an XLF dimer is sufficient for end joining in cells, but the tail of XLF must be sufficiently long to facilitate efficient end joining.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6B cellular assay

claim: The C-terminal tail of a single XLF monomer acts as a 'leash' that tethers XLF to Ku via its KBM and allows it to form required interactions with XRCC4 within the synaptic complex.
source: We propose that the C-terminal tail of a single XLF monomer acts as a 'leash' that tethers XLF to Ku via its KBM and allows it to form required interactions with XRCC4 within the synaptic complex.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental data

claim: Deleting the XLF KBM largely ablates end joining.
source: Here, we show that deleting the XLF KBM also largely ablates end joining (Figure 1C).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1C

claim: The KBM defect is likely due to a loss of XLF localization to DSBs.
source: This defect is likely due to a loss of XLF localization to DSBs, as has been observed in cells upon KBM deletion (Yano et al., 2011).
evidence: Inference from experimental data and supported by citation to Yano et al., 2011

claim: The KBM recruits XLF to DNA ends, which facilitates formation of the synaptic complex.
source: Therefore, the KBM recruits XLF to DNA ends, which facilitates formation of the synaptic complex.
evidence: Conclusion from experimental data

claim: Introduction of XLFΔKBM into cells leads to a large decrease in error-free NHEJ, although end joining remains higher than in cells lacking XLF.
source: Similar to our results in egg extract, we found that introduction of XLFΔKBM into cells leads to a large decrease in error-free NHEJ, although end joining remains higher than in cells lacking XLF (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6B cellular assay

claim: End joining could be partially rescued by high concentrations of XLFΔKBM in egg extract.
source: As end joining could be partially rescued by high concentrations of XLFΔKBM in egg extract (Figure 1D), these results suggest that XLF does not need the KBM to promote end joining when the local XLF concentration is high enough.
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 1D titration experiment

claim: XLF does not need the KBM to promote end joining when the local XLF concentration is high enough.
source: As end joining could be partially rescued by high concentrations of XLFΔKBM in egg extract (Figure 1D), these results suggest that XLF does not need the KBM to promote end joining when the local XLF concentration is high enough.
evidence: Inference from titration experiment in Figure 1D

claim: Without the KBM, XLF retains a weak residual activity that is likely mediated through its interaction with XRCC4.
source: Altogether, these findings indicate that the XLF KBM is critical for NHEJ, although without the KBM, XLF retains a weak residual activity that is likely mediated through its interaction with XRCC4.
evidence: Inference from experimental data

claim: Recruitment of XLF to DSBs is required for end joining but is not sufficient.
source: Recruitment of XLF to DSBs is required for end joining but is not sufficient.
evidence: Conclusion from experiments showing KBM and tail are both required

claim: The tail is critical for DNA end synapsis.
source: In addition to the KBM, we show that the tail is critical for DNA end synapsis (Figure 3G) and subsequent end joining in egg extract (Figure 2B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3G and Figure 2B

claim: Introducing an XLF mutant with a truncated tail that maintained the KBM (human XLF1-243+KBM) resulted in a substantial drop in NHEJ efficiency in cells.
source: Similarly, introducing an XLF mutant with a truncated tail that maintained the KBM (human XLF1-243+KBM) resulted in a substantial drop in NHEJ efficiency in cells (Figure 6B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 6B cellular assay

claim: Structural studies of XLF have commonly deleted both the tail and KBM to facilitate crystallization.
source: Structural studies of XLF have commonly deleted both the tail and KBM (Li et al., 2008; Andres et al., 2007; Andres et al., 2012; Ropars et al., 2011; Hammel et al., 2011) to facilitate crystallization (Andres et al., 2007; Andres et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple structural studies

claim: XLF constructs lacking the tail and KBM still interact with XRCC4 and promote minimal end joining in in vitro reconstitution assays.
source: This construct still interacts with XRCC4 and promotes minimal end joining in in vitro reconstitution assays (Andres et al., 2007; Hammel et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Andres et al., 2007 and Hammel et al., 2011

claim: The XLF C-terminal tail was reported to be dispensable for V(D)J recombination within human cells.
source: Within human cells, the XLF C-terminal tail was reported to be dispensable for V(D)J recombination (Malivert et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Malivert et al., 2009

claim: There may be a differential requirement of intermolecular interactions during V(D)J recombination as compared to spontaneous DSB repair.
source: As we observe a substantial reduction in NHEJ efficiency in mESCs upon removal of either the tail or KBM, this result may reflect a differential requirement of intermolecular interactions during V(D)J recombination as compared to spontaneous DSB repair.
evidence: Speculation based on comparison of results

claim: Both the flexible C-terminal tail and the KBM are required for canonical NHEJ under physiological conditions.
source: Our results demonstrate that both the flexible C-terminal tail and the KBM are required for canonical NHEJ under physiological conditions.
evidence: Conclusion from experiments in egg extract and cells

claim: Outside the KBM there are no additional motifs within the tail that are required for end joining.
source: Experiments in which we shuffled the sequence of the tail demonstrated that outside the KBM there are no additional motifs that are required for end joining (Figure 4A).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 4A with shuffled tail mutants

claim: Ablating all known and potential phosphorylation sites within the tail region did not affect end joining.
source: Similarly, ablating all known and potential phosphorylation sites within this region did not affect end joining (Figure 4A), consistent with prior results (Yu et al., 2008; Normanno et al., 2017).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 4A and supported by citations to Yu et al., 2008 and Normanno et al., 2017

claim: The length of the tail is the critical requirement for NHEJ.
source: These observations suggest that the length of the tail is the critical requirement for NHEJ and informs models of how XLF promotes end joining.
evidence: Inference from shuffled tail and phosphorylation mutant experiments

claim: A single XLF-Ku contact is sufficient for end joining.
source: These results point toward a model where a single XLF-Ku contact is sufficient for end joining.
evidence: Conclusion from asymmetric tandem dimer experiments

claim: Alternating XLF and XRCC4 filaments have been proposed to synapse DNA ends.
source: Alternating XLF and XRCC4 filaments have been proposed to synapse DNA ends and the tail of XLF has been implicated in stabilizing these filaments in vitro (Andres et al., 2012; Hammel et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citations to Andres et al., 2012 and Hammel et al., 2011

claim: XLF-XRCC4 filaments do not form during NHEJ in egg extract.
source: We disfavor this model as we have previously shown that these filaments do not form during NHEJ in egg extract (Graham et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Graham et al., 2018

claim: A single XLF dimer colocalizes with DNA shortly before the formation of the SR complex.
source: While minimal mixtures of Xenopus XLF and XRCC4 form large aggregates that bridge DNA – similar to their human homologs – quantitative single-molecule imaging showed that a single XLF dimer colocalizes with DNA shortly before the formation of the SR complex.
evidence: Supported by prior single-molecule imaging experiments

claim: Significant numbers of XLF dimers fail to accumulate on DNA indicating that filament formation does not occur during any stage of the repair reaction.
source: Furthermore, significant numbers of XLF dimers fail to accumulate on DNA indicating that filament formation does not occur during any stage of the repair reaction.
evidence: Supported by prior single-molecule imaging experiments

claim: XLF filaments are not necessary for end synapsis in human reconstitution of NHEJ.
source: Recent work in a human reconstitution of NHEJ also suggests that XLF filaments are not necessary for end synapsis (Zhao et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhao et al., 2019

claim: Lig4 is required to recruit and stabilize XRCC4 at DNA ends.
source: During repair, Lig4, which is required to recruit and stabilize XRCC4 at DNA ends (Costantini et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2007), likely blocks XLF molecules from interacting with both XRCC4 monomers thereby preventing filament formation (Recuero-Checa et al., 2009; Ochi et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Costantini et al., 2007 and Wu et al., 2007

claim: Lig4 likely blocks XLF molecules from interacting with both XRCC4 monomers thereby preventing filament formation.
source: During repair, Lig4, which is required to recruit and stabilize XRCC4 at DNA ends (Costantini et al., 2007; Wu et al., 2007), likely blocks XLF molecules from interacting with both XRCC4 monomers thereby preventing filament formation (Recuero-Checa et al., 2009; Ochi et al., 2012).
evidence: Inference supported by citations to Recuero-Checa et al., 2009 and Ochi et al., 2012

claim: A single XLF dimer is first recruited to Ku via its KBM.
source: A single XLF dimer is first recruited to Ku via its KBM.
evidence: Part of proposed model based on experimental data

claim: The tail enables XLF to find and engage with other binding partners within the complex.
source: Subsequently, the tail enables XLF to find and engage with other binding partners within the complex.
evidence: Part of proposed model based on experimental data

claim: The tail acts as a flexible connector that allows Ku-bound XLF to diffuse locally and make additional contacts that promote the transition from the LR to SR complex.
source: In this way, the tail acts as a flexible connector that allows Ku-bound XLF to diffuse locally and make additional contacts that promote the transition from the LR to SR complex.
evidence: Part of proposed model based on experimental data

claim: The XLF-XRCC4 interaction is required for NHEJ in cells.
source: One of these potential interactions is between XLF and XRCC4, an interaction that is required for NHEJ in cells (Malivert et al., 2010; Roy et al., 2015; Roy et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to Malivert et al., 2010; Roy et al., 2015; Roy et al., 2012

claim: A single XLF dimer must engage two XRCC4-Lig4 complexes, one through each head domain, for efficient SR complex formation and end joining.
source: We have previously shown that a single XLF dimer must engage two XRCC4-Lig4 complexes, one through each head domain, for efficient SR complex formation and end joining (Graham et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Graham et al., 2018

claim: A sufficient XLF tail length is required for both SR complex formation and for XLF to stabilize XRCC4-Lig4 at DNA ends.
source: Here, we demonstrate that a sufficient XLF tail length is required for both SR complex formation (Figure 3G) and for XLF to stabilize XRCC4-Lig4 at DNA ends (Figure 5B).
evidence: Demonstrated in Figure 3G and Figure 5B

claim: The tail of XLF facilitates the formation of an XLF-XRCC4 bridge that spans the DNA break or positions XRCC4-Lig4 so that Lig4 can engage the DNA ends.
source: We propose that the tail of XLF facilitates the formation of an XLF-XRCC4 bridge that spans the DNA break or positions XRCC4-Lig4 so that Lig4 can engage the DNA ends.
evidence: Proposed model based on experimental data
